**Short answer** Use the literal string `"plaintext‑only"` as the value of the `contenteditable` attribute. That is the only way to preserve the “plain‑text‑only” editing mode; converting it to `"true"` or `"false"` would lose that meaning. --- ### Why `"plaintext‑only"` is the right choice | Attribute | Standard values | Non‑standard / experimental values | |-----------|-----------------|-------------------------------------| | `contenteditable` | `"true"`, `"false"`, `"inherit"` | `"plaintext-only"` (supported by most modern browsers, but not part of the official spec) | * **`"true"`** – Enables rich‑text editing (default). * **`"false"`** – Disables editing. * **`"inherit"`** – Inherits the value from the nearest ancestor. * **`"plaintext-only"`** – Allows editing but strips out all formatting and HTML tags. This is a widely‑supported, non‑standard value that many developers use to enforce plain‑text input. Because `"plaintext-only"` is a *string value*, not a boolean, you should **not** feed it into a function that expects to map values to `"true"`/`"false"` strings. Doing so would either: 1. Return `"true"` (which would enable full rich‑text editing), or 2. Return `"false"` (which would disable editing entirely). Both outcomes would be incorrect for the intended “plain‑text‑only” behavior. --- ### How to use it in practice ```html

'true' : 'false'; } ``` --- ### Bottom line - **Keep `"plaintext-only"` as the attribute value.** - If you need a boolean string for other logic, treat `"plaintext-only"` as *truthy* (i.e., `"true"`), but **do not overwrite the attribute value** itself.
